candidates.abstract: Understanding how planets and stellar companions survive and interact with their host stars as they evolve, or are ultimately destroyed in the process, is essential both for predicting the long-term future of planetary systems like our own and the contribution of stars to galactic chemical evolution. In this white paper, we discuss how the next generation ALMA (ALMA2040) will revolutionize our understanding of the key processes by detecting and characterising accreting companions and planetary engulfment signatures in hundreds of systems with evolved stars.

candidates.title: Frontiers of chemical complexity in the interstellar medium: unveiling the cosmic origins of life
candidates.abstract: The interstellar medium (ISM) contains a rich molecular inventory that provides a unique window into the chemistry operating during star and planet formation and its connection to prebiotic chemistry. More than 350 interstellar molecules are currently known, including increasingly complex organic molecules and species containing elements beyond the second row of the periodic table. Yet the limits that interstellar chemical complexity can reach, its evolution from molecular clouds to planetary systems, and its contribution to the molecular feedstock of life remain poorly constrained. Addressing these questions requires sensitive, broadband observations capable of detecting multiple weak rotational transitions of molecular species, such as amino acids, nucleobases, sugars and lipids, towards star- and planet-forming environments. Current facilities, including ALMA, are limited by instantaneous spectral coverage, sensitivity (especially on extended spatial scales), and the trade-off between total bandwidth and integration time. The proposed ALMA2040 facility would overcome these limitations through at least a tenfold improvement in spectral-line sensitivity, high-fidelity imaging from sub-arcsecond to tens-of-arcsecond scales, and ultra-broad instantaneous frequency coverage from 35 to 950 GHz at high spectral resolution. These capabilities would allow systematic detections of species with molecular abundances with respect to H$_2$ below 10$^{-11}$, facilitating the identification of new complex and heavy-element-bearing species through multiple transitions, and providing complete molecular inventories across evolutionary stages. ALMA2040 would thus make it possible to comprehensively investigate the emergence and evolution of chemical complexity, and to determine whether molecular precursors of prebiotic chemistry are widespread throughout the Galaxy.

candidates.title: Planet formation on solar system scales
candidates.abstract: Giant planets are often regarded as primordial protoplanetary "architects". Their formation and interactions with planetesimals and other planets during and after the protoplanetary disc phase are key to setting the blueprint of the planetary systems we observe today. Catching nascent gas giants is our best opportunity to uncover these crucial steps in the planet formation process and shed light on the origins of our own solar system. Over the last decade, ALMA has revolutionised our understanding of planet formation; still, detecting signatures of Jupiter-like planets has remained out of reach. We argue that ALMA2040, a next-generation sub(mm) interferometer with improved sensitivity ($\times25$ in the continuum and $\times10$ for line emission) and a $\times3$ higher angular resolution compared to ALMA, will be sensitive to (sub)mm emission around a forming Jupiter-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star within $150\,{\rm pc}$ and allow kinematically characterising interactions of Jovian and sub-Jovian planets with their natal disc. ALMA2040 will provide unique and unprecedented insights into how gas giants carve gaps, accrete material, form satellites, and affect the architectures of their co-evolving planetary systems.

candidates.title: Star Formation across the Galaxy
candidates.abstract: Star formation is both a multi-scale and highly dynamic process. It is regulated by the combination of gravity, turbulence, feedback and magnetic fields, which connect more than six orders of magnitude in scale: from large molecular clouds (several 10s to 100s pc in size) down to protoplanetary disks (a few 10s to 100s of astronomical units in size, or 10^{-5} to 10^{-4} pc). Resolving the processes of fragmentation, accretion, and feedback that result in the formation of stellar systems throughout all relevant scales, from clouds to disks, and across the entire range of different environments in the Milky Way is key to constructing a comprehensive understanding and a predictive model of the formation process of stars of all masses that populate not only our Galaxy but the wider Universe across cosmic times. With current astronomical facilities, we are only able to grasp the details of star formation in <5% of Galactic star-forming regions, being heavily biased towards those close to us. Thus, characterizing this multi-scale phenomenon at the necessary sensitivity and resolution across all Galactic environments requires the next generation (sub)millimeter-wavelength facility: ALMA2040.

candidates.title: Multi-wavelength Polarization as a Probe of Planet Formation
candidates.abstract: Polarization reveals details of circumstellar disks that are not readily available from total intensity observations. Via multi-wavelength polarimetric observations of disks, we can trace how planets form, how dust grains evolve at the onset of planet formation, and how magnetic fields (B-fields) influence accretion. Since polarized emission from these disks is typically at levels from 0.5% to a few percent of the total emission, very high sensitivities are needed. Current ALMA capabilities make these key measurements of protoplanetary disks challenging due to (1) long integrations with separate observations to measure multi-wavelength polarization of substructures, (2) prohibitive time requests to observe large samples of disks, (3) limited sensitivity and frequency coverage for polarization in spectral lines; and (4) insufficient calibration of polarization in all the Stokes parameters. An ALMA2040 with large collecting area, increased bandwidth with multi-band capabilities, and accurate polarization calibration will provide a great leap in our understanding of the formation of protoplanets through polarization. Specifically, such an ALMA2040 can use polarized emission from the continuum and spectral lines to: (A) provide stringent tests of streaming instabilities; (B) accurately constrain grain shape, size, porosity, and alignment; (C) resolve polarization of substructures for a large sample of disks with resolutions less than 5 au; (D) quickly survey 100s of disks; and (E) measure the B-field strength and morphology of disks.

candidates.title: Chemistry on solar system scales
candidates.abstract: The initial chemical composition of planets, primitive bodies in our solar system, and exoplanets is ultimately set by their nascent protoplanetary disks. Yet observing key carbon-, oxygen-, and nitrogen-bearing molecules (as well as rarer but important sulphur- and phosphorus-bearing species) in the inner (exo)planet-forming zone ($\lesssim 10$~au) remains extremely challenging with current facilities. Therefore, to construct a complete picture of the chemistry of planet formation and understand how (exo)planetary composition is set by physical and chemical processes within the protoplanetary disk, a more powerful observing facility, i.e., ALMA2040, is needed. Compared to current ALMA (the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) this new facility must provide >~ a factor of 10 in line sensitivity at a spatial resolution of <~ 5 au at 140 pc, i.e., a factor of 3 - 4 better resolution to low surface brightness emission than currently possible. This distance includes many star-forming regions such as Taurus and Lupus that are host to populations of Sun-like stars. ALMA2040 will enable mapping of disk chemical composition on terrestrial planet-forming scales (within the water snowline) and detect molecules that are the feedstock for potentially habitable worlds.

candidates.title: Airway cross-sectional area measurement using quantitative endoscopy with AI-enabled depth estimation: A proof-of-concept study
candidates.abstract: Endoscopy is widely used in medicine to visualize anatomical structures for diagnosis and treatment evaluation. However, it does not currently allow rapid, quantitative measurement of airway cross-sectional area (CSA), a key metric for diagnosing and managing respiratory pathologies. There is growing interest in AI-enabled quantitative endoscopy using depth estimation, but a fundamental challenge is the need for ground-truth depth data to train algorithms capable of quantifying depth in physical units (e.g., meters). In this study, 60,000 paired virtual endoscopy images and depth maps were created in Blender from 3D airway models built from computed tomography. A U-Net convolutional neural network was trained to predict the depth maps from the endoscopy images. Point clouds were reconstructed from the AI-generated depth maps using the Equisolid fisheye lens model, and airway perimeters were identified by intersecting a plane with the point cloud to estimate CSA. Nasopharyngeal CSA, a key metric in obstructive sleep apnea, was quantified using this AI-enabled approach with a median error of 5.3 \% relative to the 3D model ground-truth. This pilot study using synthetic data provides strong evidence for the feasibility of developing AI-enabled quantitative endoscopy for airway CSA measurement.

candidates.title: LightHybridNet: A Lightweight Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Efficient Multi-Label Ophthalmic Disease Classification in Imbalanced Fundus Images
candidates.abstract: Eye diseases are a major global cause of blindness and vision impairment, highlighting the need for accurate and early diagnosis to prevent further deterioration. Despite advances in medical imaging, classifying retinal diseases from fundus images remains challenging due to the complexity and subtlety of visual features. This study aims to develop and validate LightHybridNet, a novel lightweight hybrid deep learning framework, to improve the classification of eye diseases from fundus images. The model incorporates architectural features, such as depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling mechanisms, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and robustness. To validate the model, the ODIR-5K dataset, comprising 8 disease categories, was used. To enhance image quality, pre-processing approaches were applied, including histogram equalisation, colour space conversion, and contrast adjustment, resulting in high-resolution images. Furthermore, image augmentation was employed to increase the dataset size, thereby improving the model's ability to generalise during training. The hybrid architecture helps the model concentrate on relevant image regions while capturing and integrating details at different scales, significantly improving classification performance. To evaluate its effectiveness, the model was compared with transfer-learning models. The results show that LightHybridNet outperforms the baselines, achieving a weighted F1-score of 91.51%, a macro AUC of 98.26%, and a Cohen's Kappa of 90.14% on the validation set. Furthermore, model interpretability was enhanced using explainable AI methods, including Grad-CAM, to identify and emphasise features influencing the decision-making process. LightHybridNet represents a promising advancement in automated ocular disease detection, offering improved diagnostic reliability for clinical use.
